title: Schrodinger did not believe his cat was really alive and dead at once.
description:
Schrodinger did not believe his cat was really alive and dead at once. He built the scenario to make that idea sound ridiculous, not to describe something he thought was true.

Published the thought experiment in the journal Naturwissenschaften, responding to Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen's paper on quantum theory from earlier that year.

In the scenario, a sealed box holds a cat alongside a radioactive atom with a fifty percent chance of triggering poison. Quantum mechanics, applied literally to the whole box, says the cat is neither alive nor dead until someone looks: a blend of both at once.

Schrodinger was arguing that this was absurd, and that something was wrong with treating a cat by the same quantum rules as a single atom. The Copenhagen interpretation he was criticising is still the one most commonly taught today.

The joke became the textbook example of the thing it was mocking.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schr%C3%B6dinger%27s_cat - confirms Erwin Schrodinger published the thought experiment in November 1935 in the journal Naturwissenschaften, in a paper written in response to the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paper published earlier that year, and states plainly that 'Schrodinger did not wish to promote the idea of dead-and-live cats as a serious possibility' but intended the example 'to illustrate the absurdity of the existing view of quantum mechanics,' employing reductio ad absurdum.
- https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/200203/history.cfm - the American Physical Society's history article corroborates that Schrodinger devised the cat scenario to expose a contradiction between quantum theory's predictions and ordinary experience, framing it as a demonstration of the theory's limitations rather than a description of how reality actually behaves.
